carrierDecision.status: AUTHOR LEANS B (extension + webview); prototype-first agreed as the way to confirm.
whyBIsViable: The 122966-byte kernel UI class implements no business logic: 14 executeCommand calls all target shuncode.* commands the extension already registers.
All 44 internal service calls have one-to-one public API equivalents; zero hits for layoutService/viewsRegistry/themeService/ICodeEditor/storageService/keybindingService/notificationService.
The author already ships two webview UIs in this same extension: workspace-hub.ts:268 (WebviewPanel) and codex-account-view.ts:14 (WebviewView).

answersToAuthorQuestions.install: Existing users install a ~2-3 MB vsix instead of reinstalling a 240 MB EXE. New users still need a full installer. B also allows shipping the extension first, which A cannot.
answersToAuthorQuestions.functionalityLoss: No business functionality is lost; the kernel class is a remote control. The only real loss is the embedding location plus visual fidelity (~90-95%, estimated not measured). Recommended placement is WebviewView (dockable sidebar), matching codex-account-view precedent.
answersToAuthorQuestions.plainVSCode: Not directly: package.json declares 7 proposed APIs (all Chat-related) that only run on a self-built carrier. A cut-down build dropping Chat integration could run on stock VS Code, keeping MCP Bridge, Skills, file tools and Workspace Hub. Separate task, not part of the B mainline.
answersToAuthorQuestions.upstreamUpgrade: Upstream = microsoft/vscode releases. A means re-applying two patch sets (workbench + sessions) on every upgrade; B relies on stable public APIs. Caveat: the 7 proposed APIs are NOT covered by compatibility guarantees, so Chat integration still tracks upstream under B.

carrierBuildProbe.headline: ANSWERED YES. With the Electron 44 clipboard adaptation restored, upstream Code OSS 1.132.0 installs and compiles cleanly against Electron 44.2.0.
carrierBuildProbe.inference: The author must have fixed these same 11 errors to ship 0.7.4, so these patches are part of the lost customisation and may be recoverable by diffing the shipped main.js.
carrierBuildProbe.harnessBugFound: The FIRST run reported npm-install failing, but that was my own defect: on Windows npm is npm.cmd and subprocess without shell=True ignores PATHEXT. Left unexamined it would have produced the false conclusion "Electron 44 cannot install". Fixed with shutil.which, plus two guards: missing tools now report harnessError/INCONCLUSIVE, and install failures are classified so network errors report INCONCLUSIVE instead of blaming Electron.
carrierBuildProbe.doesNotClaim: Compiling upstream Code OSS is not the same as rebuilding ShunCode. It proves the carrier is buildable; the author's own customisations (the extension, the Bridge UI, branding) still have to be layered on, and no installer has been produced.

keyRecoveries.BridgeActivitySnapshot: Generic in the presentation payload. Only discoverable from the author's use site (bridge-tool-dispatcher.ts:126); nothing in the JavaScript reveals the generic arity.
keyRecoveries.FileToolContext.workspaceRoots: Allowed to be a thunk, because invokeFileTool resolves it lazily so root-resolution failures are enveloped as tool errors rather than thrown. The author relies on this ('Lazy on purpose').
keyRecoveries.FileToolResult.content: Optional, evidenced by the author's `result.content ?? [...]` fallback; a mandatory field would make that dead code.
keyRecoveries.SkillLoadDiagnosis: Modelled as a discriminated union on `loaded`. The author's own code (bridge-server.ts:308-318) both maps over it and hand-builds a failing entry that still carries `name`, which is why the failure branch keeps name optional rather than omitting it.
keyRecoveries.findCustomTool: Returns CustomToolManifest | undefined - not a guess: the author's wrapper at bridge-tool-dispatcher.ts:219 declares exactly that return type. Disabled tools are invisible to it, so a caller cannot accidentally execute one.
